name: Horsetail extract

lead: Horsetail extract comes from a fern-like plant and is sold in hair and nail supplements and shampoos as a silica source. Users hope for stronger hair shafts and nails and hair that looks thicker and less brittle.

The usual proposal is silica supporting the hair shaft. Lab studies show anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity in cells, and at least two registered trials have tested multi-ingredient hair supplements; no single-ingredient hair trial was found.

paras: It is taken as a capsule or tea, or used in shampoos and tonics, usually as part of a hair-and-nail routine continued for several months.
The plant is toxic to livestock and may form nicotine in polluted conditions. Human safety data for hair-focused use are limited.

angle.text: Horsetail extract is sold in hair and nail supplements and shampoos as a silica source, with users hoping for a stronger hair shaft and thicker, less brittle hair. Lab data exist, and single-ingredient hair trials were not found.

lead: Horsetail extract is prepared from Equisetum arvense (field or common horsetail), a perennial non-flowering plant native to northern temperate regions [1]. It is marketed in hair and nail supplements and shampoos as a source of silica, with the plant reported to contain silicon along with flavonoids, saponins, tannins and minerals [1].

Wikipedia describes evidence for its medicinal properties as limited, with laboratory data suggesting anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and antimicrobial activity [1]. No published human trial reviewed here has shown an effect of horsetail alone on hair growth, though at least two registered trials have tested multi-ingredient hair supplements [2][3].

paras: Austrian herbal tradition used horsetail tea, baths and compresses for skin, kidney and joint complaints, Finnish folk medicine valued its silicic acid, and it was historically used to strengthen fingernails [1]. The plant has also been used to polish pewter and wood because of its abrasive stems [1].

A laboratory study of a standardized commercial E. arvense extract reported effects on human lymphocyte function in vitro, consistent with the plant's European use for inflammatory disorders [4]. A rat study reported SIRT1-related effects on insulin sensitivity in induced diabetes [5]. A 2025 qualitative review of alopecia misinformation is among the literature that discusses unproven hair remedies [6].
Wikipedia notes that horsetail is toxic to livestock, particularly horses, and that the plant may synthesize nicotine under polluted conditions [1].
No studies found of horsetail extract on its own for hair loss or hair growth in humans.

Two registered trials, NCT06841458 (n=45, androgenetic alopecia, recruiting) and NCT06174441 (n=89, hair thinning, completed 2024), test dietary supplements for hair; the listings reviewed here do not establish horsetail as a sole active ingredient, and no results are summarized [2][3].

lore.intro: Horsetail is mentioned in hair-supplement marketing and natural-hair discussions mainly as a silica source.
